question: Give an example of working productively with someone you personally disagreed with or found difficult.

raiseTranscript.text: I disagreed with a senior engineer on the right approach for a feature. I thought we should use a simpler library; he wanted a more robust but heavier one.
What did you do next?

I scheduled a 30-minute chat, shared my concerns with a quick prototype, and asked for his reasoning. We ended up using his approach after he showed me edge cases I had missed. I documented the decision.
How did it feel afterward?
Still not my first choice, but the feature shipped cleanly and I learned two patterns I now reuse.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of working productively with someone you personally disagreed with.
Situation: disagreed with senior engineer on library choice for a feature
Action: booked short meeting, brought prototype and questions, accepted decision after discussion
Outcome: feature shipped cleanly; candidate reused two patterns later
Quote: "I documented the decision."
Follow-up: Asked how it felt afterward - candidate described learning without resentment
junior.raiseFeedback: The story shows the candidate owning their part of the disagreement and using a direct, low-drama conversation to resolve it. They brought a concrete artifact (prototype) rather than just opinions. The outcome stayed local to one feature but included clear personal learning. This meets the bar for junior because the focus is on individual coachability and completing the work rather than heroics. Biggest strength is the willingness to accept a different decision once evidence was shared.

lowerTranscript.text: There was a teammate who kept rejecting my PRs. I thought his standards were too high so I just stopped asking him for review and went to someone else.
Did you ever talk to him directly?
Not really. I mentioned it to my manager once but nothing changed so I worked around it.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of working productively with someone you personally disagreed with.
Situation: teammate rejecting PRs
Action: avoided the reviewer and routed around him
Outcome: work continued but no resolution
Quote: "I just stopped asking him for review."
Follow-up: Asked if they spoke directly - candidate had not attempted a conversation
junior.lowerFeedback: The candidate chose avoidance over any attempt at direct resolution. No evidence of trying to understand the other person's concerns or adjusting their own behavior. The result was local work completion without growth or improved working relationship. This lowers the bar for junior because even at this level we expect basic ownership of interpersonal friction rather than escalation or workarounds.

raiseTranscript.text: A PM on another team kept pushing scope that conflicted with our reliability goals. I disagreed strongly with the priority.
How did you handle it?

I asked for a joint planning session, brought latency data from the last two releases, and proposed two scope options that met both needs. We aligned on one and I wrote the follow-up note that both teams used.
What was the measurable result?
The feature launched with p99 under target and the PM later asked me to review two other roadmaps.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of working productively with someone you personally disagreed with.
Situation: PM pushing scope against reliability goals
Action: initiated joint session with data, offered two options, wrote shared follow-up
Outcome: launch met targets; PM began seeking input on other work
Quote: "I wrote the follow-up note that both teams used."
Follow-up: Asked for measurable result - candidate cited p99 and ongoing cross-team requests
senior.raiseFeedback: The candidate used data and a structured meeting to surface the conflict without making it personal. They created a shared artifact that gave both sides a path forward. Impact extended beyond their own team when the PM started seeking their input elsewhere. This raises the bar for senior because it demonstrates influence without authority and a repeatable cross-team pattern rather than one-off heroics.

lowerTranscript.text: I disagreed with a PM on priorities. I sent a long email explaining why their plan was risky and copied my manager.
We had one meeting but it stayed tense. I focused on getting my concerns on record so the decision was documented.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of working productively with someone you personally disagreed with.
Situation: disagreement with PM on priorities
Action: sent detailed email with manager copied
Outcome: one tense meeting; focus remained on documentation
Quote: "I focused on getting my concerns on record."
Follow-up: Asked if they met to discuss - candidate described email-first approach
senior.lowerFeedback: The candidate defaulted to written escalation and documentation rather than attempting real-time resolution. The meeting that followed stayed adversarial because no shared options were prepared. No evidence of later improved collaboration. This lowers the bar for senior because we expect seniors to drive alignment across teams, not simply protect themselves with paper trails.

raiseTranscript.text: Two engineers on my team had ongoing friction over code ownership that was slowing reviews.
What steps did you take?

I met each one separately first to hear their view, then brought them together with a clear agenda. We defined explicit ownership boundaries and a lightweight escalation path. I checked in weekly for a month and adjusted once based on their feedback.
How did the team change?
Review time dropped and both engineers later volunteered to pair on a new service.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of working productively with someone you personally disagreed with.
Situation: two engineers with ownership friction slowing reviews
Action: separate 1:1s, joint meeting with agenda, defined boundaries and escalation, weekly check-ins
Outcome: faster reviews; both engineers later paired together
Quote: "I checked in weekly for a month and adjusted once based on their feedback."
Follow-up: Asked how the team changed - candidate cited measurable review time and voluntary pairing
manager.raiseFeedback: The manager invested time in understanding each person's perspective before facilitating a structured conversation. They created lasting process changes and followed up to refine them. The result included both faster delivery and improved working relationship between the two engineers. This raises the bar for manager because it shows deliberate development of team dynamics rather than just resolving the immediate conflict.

lowerTranscript.text: I had two engineers who didn't get along. I told them to work it out and reassigned a couple of tickets so they interacted less.
Not really. The tickets got done and the noise went down so I moved on to other issues.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of working productively with someone you personally disagreed with.
Situation: two engineers with interpersonal friction
Action: told them to work it out and reduced their interaction via ticket reassignment
Outcome: immediate noise reduced but no lasting resolution
Quote: "The tickets got done and the noise went down so I moved on."
Follow-up: Asked if they followed up - candidate had not
manager.lowerFeedback: The manager avoided coaching the individuals and chose structural separation instead of addressing the root behavior. No follow-up occurred once the visible symptoms decreased. Team dynamics were not improved. This lowers the bar for manager because the role requires developing people through conflict, not routing around it.

raiseTranscript.text: Two directors were in open conflict over investment priorities between two product lines, blocking a reorg decision.
How did you approach it?

I met each director one-on-one to map their constraints and incentives, then ran a joint offsite with pre-read data on customer impact and revenue. We landed on a phased investment model and I made the final call publicly with both directors' input acknowledged.
What was the longer-term effect?
The reorg launched on schedule and the two directors later co-sponsored a joint initiative that neither had supported before.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of working productively with someone you personally disagreed with.
Situation: two directors blocking reorg over investment priorities
Action: separate mapping meetings, joint offsite with data, public decision acknowledging both inputs
Outcome: reorg on schedule; later joint sponsorship of new initiative
Quote: "I made the final call publicly with both directors' input acknowledged."
Follow-up: Asked for longer-term effect - candidate described cross-initiative collaboration
exec.raiseFeedback: The executive invested in understanding underlying incentives before creating a structured forum for resolution. They owned the final decision while preserving dignity for both parties. The result included both timely organizational change and new collaborative behavior between the leaders. This raises the bar for exec because it shows strategic use of conflict to unlock larger business movement rather than just settling a dispute.

lowerTranscript.text: Two leaders disagreed on direction. I listened to both sides, made a decision, and communicated it in the staff meeting.
Did you do anything to align them beforehand?
I had separate conversations but kept them short because the decision needed to be made quickly.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of working productively with someone you personally disagreed with.
Situation: two leaders disagreeing on direction
Action: separate short conversations then unilateral decision announced in staff meeting
Outcome: decision communicated but no evidence of alignment
Quote: "I kept them short because the decision needed to be made quickly."
Follow-up: Asked if they worked to align beforehand - candidate described minimal pre-work
exec.lowerFeedback: The executive treated the conflict as a decision to be made rather than a relationship to be managed. Minimal investment in surfacing constraints or creating shared ownership led to a top-down outcome. No follow-on collaboration was reported. This lowers the bar for exec because senior leaders are expected to convert disagreement into organizational leverage, not simply decide and move on.
